answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From ‘Il Principe’ (‘The Prince’), Chapter 17, written c. 1513 and first published 1532. This exact English wording is Luigi Ricci’s 1903 translation ↗ — the underlying idea is authentically Machiavelli’s.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Concerning Cruelty and Clemency, and Whether it is Better to be Loved than Feared”

source.excerpt: The reply is, that one ought to be both feared and loved, but as it is difficult for the two to go together, it is much safer to be feared than loved, if one of the two has to be wanting. For it may be said of men in general that they are ungrateful, voluble, dissemblers, anxious to avoid danger, and covetous of gain.
trail: The exact phrasing appears verbatim in Luigi Ricci’s 1903 translation of ch. 17 ↗.
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced section ↗, cited to The Prince (1513), ch. 17, Ricci translation.
Chapter 17’s theme — whether a ruler should prefer love or fear — is confirmed by the USF Lit2Go text of ch. 17 ↗.
source.excerptNote: Luigi Ricci’s 1903 English translation of ‘Il Principe’, ch. 17. “Wanting” here means lacking or absent.

sourceLink.text: The Prince (Ricci translation), Chapter 17 on Wikisource

source.rightsNote: The Italian original of ‘Il Principe’ (first published 1532) is long in the public domain, and Luigi Ricci’s English translation was first published in 1903 — well before 1931 — so this specific rendering is also public domain in the United States.

author.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
author.heading: About Machiavelli
author.metaLine: 1469–1527 · Florentine political philosopher, diplomat & author of The Prince
author.bio: Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, historian and political theorist whose 1513 treatise Il Principe (‘The Prince’) became the founding text of modern political realism. Written after the Medici returned to power and stripped him of office, it advises rulers on acquiring and holding power by any effective means. Chapter 17 — on cruelty, clemency, and whether it is better to be loved or feared — is the source of this line.

misattribution.heading: A real quote, often mangled
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Machiavelli is correct — but the line circulates in many altered forms, and the popular version is usually a loose paraphrase rather than this precise wording.

items.who: “It is better to be feared than loved, if you cannot be both.”
items.why: This truncated form swaps Ricci’s “much safer” for “better” and “if one of the two has to be wanting” for “if you cannot be both.” It captures the sense but is not the wording of any single standard translation; Ricci’s actual text ↗ reads differently.

Machiavelli immediately qualifies the line, warning that a prince must avoid being hated even while feared — a nuance dropped when the sentence is quoted as a standalone maxim, as the full chapter shows ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Machiavelli’s; this exact English form is Luigi Ricci’s 1903 translation of ‘The Prince’, ch. 17 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Machiavelli wrote ‘The Prince’ around 1513, after the collapse of the Florentine republic he had served returned the Medici to power and cost him his post. The book’s advice — that a ruler should be guided by what works rather than by conventional virtue — made his name a byword for cold political calculation.

In Chapter 17 he weighs whether a prince should court love or fear. Because human loyalty is fickle, he argues, fear is the more reliable foundation — yet he tempers this at once, insisting the prince must never become hated.
